content_of_post_to_comment: Reading Günther Anders’ long essay on radio and television from the 1950s, I’m struck by his fixation on a particular piece of furniture: the table. Anders sees the television—what he calls the table’s “true successor” in the modern household—as “a family table in reverse”, directing the attention not inward towards the space the family has in common, but outward towards the screen that connects each of them with a mass society: “Whereas the table had made the family centripetal—it had forced family members to continue weaving the fabric of family life by making the shuttles of looks, interests, and words run back and forth—the screen now gives it a centrifugal orientation.” Compare this to what Hannah Arendt writes in The Human Condition: “The public realm, as the common world, gathers us together and yet prevents our falling over each other, so to speak. What makes mass society so difficult to bear is not the number of people involved, or at least not primarily, but the fact that the world between them has lost its power to gather them together, to relate and separate them. The weirdness of this situation resembles a spiritualistic séance where a number of people gathered around a table might suddenly, through some magic trick, see the table vanish from their midst, so that two persons sitting opposite each other were no longer separated but also would be entirely unrelated to each other by anything tangible.” Arendt and Anders were married from 1929 to 1937, and one wonders about the sorts of conversations they may have had during those years which seem to have left a mark on each of their later writing—very likely, or so I imagine, as the two of them were seated together at a table.
comment: The table’s disappearance suggests more than a loss of togetherness: it may be a loss of friction. Shared spaces once forced encounters with difference; screens let us curate proximity without the inconvenience of negotiation.
